Carbonyl iron powder with particle size mostly between 4-7 micrometers is used as magnetic filler.
EPDM rubber serves as the matrix material for the radar absorbing material.
Effective complex magnetic permeability and dielectric permittivity increase with carbonyl iron volume fraction.
Reflection loss decreases from -1.3 dB to -23.9 dB as carbonyl iron volume fraction increases from 0 to 0.45 at 3.0 mm thickness.
Frequency of minimum reflection loss shifts from 15.5 GHz to 3.5 GHz with increasing carbonyl iron content.
Increasing RAM thickness shifts the minimum reflection loss frequency to lower bands but reflection loss is not proportional to thickness.
Two dielectric loss peaks at approximately 9.0 GHz and 15.0 GHz correspond to relaxation polarization and electric conductance losses.
Pure EPDM rubber shows nearly constant dielectric permittivity (~1) and magnetic permeability (~2.5) with negligible losses.
Impedance matching degree is defined as the normalized input impedance ratio between RAM surface and free space.
Optimal impedance matching minimizes reflection loss and maximizes microwave absorption.
Reflection loss bandwidth at -10 dB is about 4.0 GHz for carbonyl iron volume fractions of 0.3 and 0.45.
The RAM samples were prepared by mixing fillers and matrix in a two-roll mixer, vulcanized at 140 °C for 10 minutes.
Measurements were conducted using an HP8722ET vector network analyzer and APC-7 coaxial transmission line.
Magnetic loss increases with frequency due to magnetic retardation effects.
The RAM is a metal-backed single-layer absorber designed to reduce electromagnetic wave reflection by impedance matching.
Carbonyl iron has a high Curie temperature and good temperature stabilization, favorable for RAM applications.
The reflection loss depends on a combination of six parameters including complex permeability, permittivity, thickness, frequency, and wave properties.
The study confirms that increasing carbonyl iron content and optimizing thickness improves microwave absorption performance.
The dielectric permittivity and magnetic permeability of the RAM do not follow simple linear mixing laws due to differences between matrix and filler materials.
The RAM shows a single-peaked reflection loss curve with peak absorption frequency decreasing as carbonyl iron content or thickness increases.
